title: The Khamaṇa's Wife
summary: A woman married to a khamaṇa says her bigoā cannot be told; in the refrain she tells her mother that she has broken away and that what she carried here is not here, and she goes on to a first birth wrapped in habitual tendencies, an examined channel, her youth come to fullness, the root torn out and the father destroyed. Munidatta makes the speaker the goddess Nairātmā, whose husband is the wholly empty mind (cp.20.m1, cp.20.m2), and reads the later couplets as examination, the fruit of practice and direct realization, with the root as conventional bodhicitta (cp.20.m4 to cp.20.m6).

flags.note: The poet's name is not in this heading line: the edition writes the attribution kukkurīpādānām, 'of Kukkurīpāda', before the song, and the input moves it out of line 1a as not part of the verse. I have put it in the heading, in the form the brief gives for headings; the Tibetan heading also names him (kuk+ku rI'i zhabs).

lines.gloss: I · without desire (or: without hope) · with a khamaṇa-husband
lines.en: I am without desire, with a [khamaṇa]{khamana} [husband]{husband}.

flags.note: nirāsī (feminine, so the speaker is a woman): I take it as nirāśī, 'without wishes, without desire' (compare Sanskrit nirāśis). The everyday sense of nirāśa is 'hopeless, forlorn', which would make the couplet a wife's lament; 'homeless' (as if from nir-āvāsa) is a remoter possibility. The commentary's 'free of attachment' (nirāsā, āsaṅgarahitā, cp.20.m2) and the Tibetan chags med, 'without attachment', lean toward my choice.
khamaṇabhatāre: the -e ending may be instrumental ('with, or because of, a khamaṇa husband') or nominative ('my husband is a khamaṇa'); 'with a khamaṇa husband' keeps both open.
khamaṇa is kept in source form, as the glossary asks: kha 'sky' + maṇa 'mind' (so the Tibetan line, nam mkha'i yid, 'sky-mind'), or Prakrit khamaṇa, 'Jain ascetic' (Sanskrit kṣapaṇa).

lines.translit: mohora bigoā kahaṇa na jāi || dhru ||
lines.gloss: my · bigoā · telling · not · goes (= cannot be told) · (refrain cue)

flags.note: bigoā is of uncertain sense and is kept in source form, as the glossary asks. The Tibetan line has nyams myong, 'experience', and the commentary's paraphrase has 'my experience of imperishable bliss' in its place (cp.20.m2). A link with a verb 'spoil, ruin, disgrace' (compare Sanskrit vi-gup, causative vigopayati) would give 'plight' or 'undoing', which suits a wife's complaint; I cannot confirm it.
Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after this couplet as well as after couplet 2. Munidatta names couplet 2 as the refrain (dhrupada, cp.20.m3), and the input marks it so. The cue is not translated.

lines.translit: pheṭaliu go māe anta uṛi cāhi
lines.gloss: broke away (I; past of pheṭ-/phiṭ-) · (vocative particle) · mother · end · up (or: flying) · look
lines.en: I broke away, O [mother]{mother}; I look up to the end.

flags.note: pheṭaliu is apparently a first-person past of pheṭ-/phiṭ-, 'split, burst, be severed, be removed'; I render it 'broke away'. Both other witnesses make it transitive: the commentary has 'cut off by me' (niṣkṛntita), with the host of sense objects as object, and perhaps glosses the verb itself as sphuṭam, 'burst open' (cp.20.m3); the Tibetan has spangs nas, 'having abandoned', with khyod, 'you'. 'I burst open' and 'I cast it off' are the main alternatives.
Shastri's footnote: the song has pheṭaliu, while the commentary cites phiṭalesu (cp.20.m3). Both look like past forms of one verb, and the difference does not change the rendering.

anta uṛi cāhi: anta is 'end, edge, limit' (Munidatta's paryanta, cp.20.m3; the Tibetan mtha' ma); uṛi is 'up' or 'flying'; cāhi is 'look', as both witnesses take it, or 'want', which would give 'I want to fly to the end'. I follow the witnesses.
The Tibetan line (kye'i mi khyod spangs nas mtha' mar lta) has no mother: its vocative seems to fall on mi, 'person, man', and it has a 'you' (khyod) that the Bengali lacks.

lines.translit: jāethu bāhāma so ethu nāhi || dhru ||
lines.gloss: what here · I carried (bāh-) · that · here · is not · (refrain cue)
lines.en: What I carried here is not here.

flags.note: bāhāma is a first person of bāh- (Sanskrit vah-, 'carry, bear', also 'flow'). 'Carried' keeps the literal verb; 'bore' would press a childbirth sense. The Tibetan has 'bab pa, 'flows down' ('whatever flows down here is not here'), and the commentary paraphrases 'whatever enemy, sense object, I look at here, none of them exists' (cp.20.m3).

lines.gloss: first · birth (biāṇa) · my · wrapped in vāsanā (bāsanapūṛa)
lines.en: My first [birth]{biana} was wrapped in [habitual tendencies]{vasana}.

flags.note: Shastri's footnote: the manuscript's song text reads bāsanabuṛa, and he printed bāsanapūṛa after the commentary's vāsanāpuṭa (cp.20.m4), so the printed word has been brought into line with the commentary. I translate the printed text because the Tibetan line, an independent witness, has gtums, 'wrapped', which fits puṭa, 'wrapping, pouch'. The manuscript's buṛa may mean 'sunk' (compare Bengali buṛ-, 'sink'), giving 'sunk in habitual tendencies'. The English changes little either way.

biāṇa: I take it as 'birth, bringing forth' (compare Bengali biyāna, used of animals giving birth), which Munidatta's 'this body was born' (prasūta, cp.20.m4) supports. The Tibetan line reads rnam shes, 'consciousness', as if biāṇa were vijñāna: 'at first my consciousness was wrapped in habitual tendencies'. 'Birth' leaves open whether the speaker was born or gave birth.
bāsana is rendered by the glossary's 'habitual tendencies' (vāsanā). The spelling would also allow vāsana, 'box, vessel', or vasana, 'garment'; I have not followed these.

lines.gloss: channel (nāṛi) · on examining · that very · poor wretch · (refrain cue)
lines.en: On [examination]{vicara} of the [channel]{nadi}, that same [poor wretch]{bapura}.

flags.note: The line has no verb, and I have left it elliptical. Munidatta takes it as a rhetorical question: how could that wretched vāsanā exist? It does not (cp.20.m4). The song itself only sets 'that same poor wretch' against the examination.

Shastri's footnote: for bāpūṛā the commentary has varākī (feminine, qualifying vāsanā, cp.20.m4), and he notes that bāpuṛāi should be the form. As printed, masculine or unmarked, 'poor wretch' could point to a person: the husband, or the one born. seba is 'that very' (the commentary's saiva, the Tibetan de nyid). The Tibetan transliterates bāpūṛā (ba pu DA) instead of translating it.

nāṛi is rendered by the glossary's 'channel' (nāḍī), as Munidatta and the Tibetan (rtsa) take it (cp.20.m4). The Old Bengali word is also the pulse a physician feels and the navel cord, and 'examining the nāṛi' is the ordinary phrase for taking a pulse. Singular or plural is not marked.

lines.en: Know: my [youth]{yauvana} has come to fullness.

flags.note: Shastri's footnote: the manuscript's song text has জাণজৌবন (jāṇajaubana), written as one word; the commentary cites navayauvana, 'fresh youth' (cp.20.m5); the Tibetan has gzhon nu dar ma, 'youthful prime', with no separate word, which may also reflect nava. Shastri printed the song's jāṇa as a word of its own. I take jāṇa as the imperative 'know', which I understand song 1's refrain to use ('ask the guru and know'); please check. Alternatively jāṇa is jñāna, 'knowledge', in a compound: 'my youth of knowledge has come to fullness'.

lines.gloss: root · having torn out (nakhali) · father · destroyed · (refrain cue)

flags.note: nakhali is of uncertain sense. I take it as an absolutive, 'having torn out', perhaps from nakha, 'nail' ('clawed out'), or akin to a verb 'pull out'; Munidatta has nikṛtti, 'cutting' (cp.20.m5). saṃghārā is saṃhāra, 'destruction'. The subject is unexpressed; the commentary makes it 'me, Kukkurīpāda' (cp.20.m5). I have kept the verbless shape.

The Tibetan line, rtsa bar ltung ba nye bar sdud par byed, 'gathers up (or withdraws) what fell at the root', has no father. nye bar sdud usually renders (upa)saṃhāra, 'withdrawal', so the translators seem to have read saṃghārā in that sense; ltung ba, 'fall', may stand for bāpa read as some other word. The father is also absent from Munidatta's comment (cp.20.m5).

bhaba thirā may be a statement ('existence is steady') or elliptical for 'having made existence steady', as Munidatta explains sthira (sthiraṃ kṛtvā, cp.20.m6). The Tibetan, kuk+ku rI pa'i srid pa brtan par smra, 'Kukkurīpa speaks of existence as steady', agrees with the statement.

lines.translit: jo ethu bujhaem̐ so ethu bīrā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: who · here · understands · he · here · hero · (refrain cue)
lines.en: Whoever understands here is a [hero]{vira} here.

flags.note: ethu … ethu, 'here … here', echoes the refrain (jāethu … so ethu nāhi), so I keep both. The first ethu could instead be the object, 'this' ('whoever understands this'), as the Tibetan takes it ('di ni gang shes, 'whoever knows this').

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. The heading names the rāga to which the song is sung, Paṭamañjarī, which is also the melody of song 1.

Nirāsī is feminine, so the speaker is a woman. It can mean 'without wishes, without desire' (compare Sanskrit nirāśis) or, in its everyday sense, 'hopeless, forlorn'; this draft takes the first. Khamaṇa, the word she uses of her husband, is of uncertain sense and is kept in source form. It can be divided as kha, 'sky', and maṇa, 'mind', as the Tibetan line does (nam mkha'i yid, 'sky-mind'), or read as Prakrit khamaṇa, a Jain ascetic (Sanskrit kṣapaṇa), which would make her the wife of a monk.

Bigoā is of uncertain sense and derivation and is kept in source form. The Tibetan line has nyams myong, 'experience'. A derivation from a verb meaning 'spoil, ruin' (compare Sanskrit vigopayati) would give 'plight' or 'undoing'. Mohora is 'my', not moha, 'delusion'.

Munidatta says that Kukkurīpāda, content from drinking the nectar of the meaning of the perfection of wisdom, speaks having resolved on himself as that very meaning, the Blessed Lady Nairātmā yoginī (cp.20.m1). So the 'I' of the song is Nairātmā: nirāsī means she is free of attachment; khamaṇa is the wholly empty mind, her lord; and through attachment to lovemaking with him, her experience of the imperishable bliss of distinguished union cannot be known through speech (cp.20.m2). He supports this with an Apabhraṃśa verse of Saraha whose text is partly corrupt. Where the Sanskrit has lovemaking (surata, partly restored by Shastri), the Tibetan comment has 'great bliss' (shin du bde ba).

Pheṭaliu (the commentary cites it as phiṭalesu) seems to be a first-person past of a verb meaning 'split, burst, be severed'. Munidatta's paraphrase has 'cut off by me' (niṣkṛntita) and, perhaps as a gloss on the verb, sphuṭam, 'burst open, plain' (cp.20.m3); the Tibetan has spangs nas, 'having abandoned'. Anta is 'end, edge, limit', uṛi 'up' or 'flying', cāhi 'look'.

Munidatta says the refrain confirms the same meaning. Anta, 'end', is the limit: Nairātmā has seen her own hut, the wheel of great bliss, and at that time she cut off the host of sense objects. Addressing herself as 'O mother, Nairātmā', she says that whatever enemy, sense object, she now looks at here, none of them exists, since everything is made of great bliss (cp.20.m3). The Tibetan comment breaks off after 'removed' (sel ba).

The Tibetan refrain reads kye'i mi khyod spangs nas mtha' mar lta / gang zhig 'dir na 'bab pa de 'dir med, roughly 'O man, you … having abandoned, look to the end; whatever flows down here is not here'. It has no mother, adds a 'you', and takes bāhāma as 'flows down' ('bab pa).

Shastri notes that the manuscript's song text has bāsanabuṛa; he printed bāsanapūṛa, following the commentary's vāsanāpuṭa, 'casket of tendencies' (cp.20.m4). Buṛa may mean 'sunk' ('sunk in tendencies'); pūṛa may come from puṭa, 'wrapping, pouch'. The Tibetan line, dang por bdag gi rnam shes bag chags gtums, 'at first my consciousness was wrapped in tendencies', supports a word meaning 'wrapped', but reads biāṇa as consciousness (rnam shes, for vijñāna).

Biāṇa is taken here as 'birth, bringing forth' (compare Bengali biyāna, used of animals giving birth); Munidatta's paraphrase, 'this body was born' (prasūta), fits it (cp.20.m4). The line does not say whether the speaker was born or gave birth.

Nāṛi is any tube or vein: the channels of yoga, the pulse a physician examines, the navel cord. Bāpūṛā, 'poor wretch', is a word of pity or contempt; as printed it is not feminine, so it need not refer to the tendencies of the line before.

For bāpūṛā the commentary has varākī, agreeing with vāsanā (cp.20.m4), and Shastri notes that the feminine bāpuṛāi should be the form. The Tibetan line, rtsa la rnam dpyod de nyid ba pu DA, 'examining the channel, that very ba pu ḍā', leaves the word untranslated.

Munidatta calls this couplet his 'second verse', on the nature of examination (vicāra). At first this body was born as a casket of conventional tendencies; its channels are the thirty-two goddesses; when they are examined in the order of the piṇḍīkrama, on the authority of the true guru's words, that wretched vāsanā is not found at all (cp.20.m4). The Tibetan translation has no comment on this couplet.

Shastri notes that the manuscript's song text has jāṇajaubana, written as one word, where the commentary has navayauvana, 'fresh youth' (cp.20.m5). The Tibetan line, bdag ni gzhon nu dar ma rdzogs par gyur, 'my youthful prime became complete', has no word for jāṇa. This draft takes jāṇa as the imperative 'know'; it may instead be jñāna, 'knowledge' ('my youth of knowledge').

Nakhali is of uncertain sense: perhaps 'clawed out' (from nakha, 'nail') or 'pulled out'; Munidatta has nikṛtti, 'cutting' (cp.20.m5). Saṃghārā is saṃhāra, 'destruction'. Bāpa, 'father', is a different word from bāpūṛā, 'poor wretch', in 3b.

The Tibetan line, rtsa bar ltung ba nye bar sdud par byed, 'gathers up what fell at the root', has no father. Its nye bar sdud usually renders upasaṃhāra, 'withdrawal', perhaps for saṃghārā; Munidatta also speaks of the withdrawal of the sphere of sense objects in his comment on this couplet (cp.20.m5). Of that comment the Tibetan keeps only the last sentence.

Munidatta calls this couplet his 'third verse', on the fruit of practice (abhyāsa). The root is conventional bodhicitta, and its cutting was done 'by me, Kukkurīpāda, meditating on selflessness', at the root of the jewel. Fresh youth is made by the withdrawal of the sphere of sense objects, and by its power, he tells himself, 'O body-vajra, you have become beautiful with the body of the great Vajradhara, with the thirty-two marks and eighty signs' (cp.20.m5). Here the speaker is Kukkurīpāda, not Nairātmā as in his comments on couplets 1 and 2. He quotes a line he attributes to the Hevajra (tīradvayaṃ bhaved ghaṇṭāṃ) whose wording looks corrupt, and he does not mention the father.

Munidatta calls this couplet his 'fourth verse', on direct realization (sākṣātkāra). The existence of the line is conventional bodhicitta; 'steady' means having made it steady; the steadfast lords of yogis who have understood it in stainless form are heroes in this circle of existence, because they crush the enemy, the sense objects. He closes with a line of Kṛṣṇācārya on understanding the uninterrupted innate moment (cp.20.m6).

Taken literally, the song is spoken by a woman married to a khamaṇa, who addresses her mother. Several of its words suit a scene of childbirth: biāṇa, 'birth'; nāṛi, which is also the navel cord; and the refrain's 'what I carried here is not here'. None of them is certain, and the song names no child. The father destroyed in 4b is a violent paradox, like the killing of the mother in song 11.

termsOmitted.reason: False hit: mohora is the first-person genitive 'my' (the Tibetan has bdag gi), not moha, 'delusion'.
Hit in the Tibetan line only: rtsa ba there is 'root', rendering mūla, not rtsa, 'channel'.
Hit in the Tibetan line only (nye bar sdud), apparently the translators' reading of saṃghārā; the Bengali line has 'destroyed', and the Tibetan reading is reported in a witness note.

proposals.definition: Old Bengali biāṇa, taken here as 'birth, bringing forth' (compare Bengali biyāna, used of animals giving birth). In song 20 (3a) the speaker's first biāṇa is wrapped in habitual tendencies. Munidatta's paraphrase has 'this body was born' (prasūta) (cp.20.m4); the Tibetan line reads rnam shes, 'consciousness', as if the word were vijñāna.
proposals.symbolicImage: the speaker's first birth, wrapped in habitual tendencies

symbolicReadings.referent: this body (kāya), born at first as a casket of conventional habitual tendencies (saṃvṛtivāsanāpuṭa); his paraphrase puts it where the song has 'my first birth', without an explicit gloss

proposals.rationale: The word carries couplet 3, and the witnesses disagree about it (birth in the commentary, consciousness in the Tibetan); an entry keeps the rendering consistent and records the alternatives. The Tibetan rnam shes is left out of the forms because it is the ordinary word for vijñāna and would over-match.

proposals.definition: Old Bengali bāpuṛā, 'poor wretch, wretched' (Sanskrit varāka), a word of pity or contempt. In song 20 (3b) it closes the examination of the channel. Munidatta renders it varākī, qualifying vāsanā (cp.20.m4); Shastri notes the feminine bāpuṛāi as the expected form, and the Tibetan transliterates it. Not bāpa, 'father'.
proposals.symbolicImage: that same poor wretch, set against the examination of the channel

symbolicReadings.referent: the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) themselves, 'that very wretched vāsanā', which is not found at all when the body's channels, the thirty-two goddesses, are examined

proposals.rationale: The glossary's father entry warns against confusing bāpa with bāpūṛā; an entry for the latter makes the distinction markable and records the commentary's feminine varākī and Shastri's note.

questions: Heading: I added '· Kukkurīpāda' from the attribution the edition writes before the song (the input moved it out of 1a). Keep it, or leave the heading as the bare rāga name?

3a: the printed bāsanapūṛa is Shastri's correction from the commentary (vāsanāpuṭa); the manuscript's song text has bāsanabuṛa. I translated the printed text ('wrapped in') because the Tibetan gtums, 'wrapped', supports it. Would you rather translate the manuscript ('sunk in habitual tendencies') and put Shastri's reading in the note?

4a: I read jāṇa as the imperative 'know' ('Know: my youth has come to fullness'), on the model of what I take to be the imperative jāṇa in song 1's refrain; please check that line. The alternative is jñāna, 'knowledge' ('my youth of knowledge'). The commentary's navayauvana and the Tibetan's 'youthful prime' do not decide it.
3b: the glossary's 'channel' for nāṛi puts a yogic word into the verse, where the Old Bengali may mean a pulse or the navel cord. Keep 'channel', or allow a plainer 'vein' in this line?

3a: biāṇa as 'birth' (with Munidatta's prasūta) against the Tibetan 'consciousness' (rnam shes). I have proposed an entry (biana). Is 'birth' acceptable, or should the word stay in source form, like bigoā?
1a: nirāsī as 'without desire' (nirāśis, and the commentary's 'free of attachment') or 'without hope' (the everyday sense, which makes the opening a wife's lament)?

2a: 'I broke away' renders pheṭaliu intransitively; both other witnesses make it transitive (the commentary 'cut off', the Tibetan 'abandoned you'). Would you prefer 'I cast it off', or 'I burst open'?
The glossary's 'habitual tendencies' for vāsanā is heavy in a sung line. Is a shorter variant such as 'tendencies' acceptable in the verse?
The unit-level imagery note says several words suit a childbirth scene. Is that too much for a note, given that none of the words is certain?
